pathophysiology.summary: Pre-eclampsia is a placental disorder: abnormal remodelling of the spiral arteries leads to placental ischaemia, which releases anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1, low placental growth factor) that cause widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction — hypertension, proteinuria and multi-organ injury.
keyMechanisms: Endothelial dysfunction → vasoconstriction, capillary leak (oedema, pulmonary oedema), platelet activation and coagulation (HELLP, DIC).
Low placental growth factor (PlGF) reflects placental dysfunction — PlGF-based testing helps rule out pre-eclampsia (20 to 36+6 weeks).

Organ involvement: kidney (creatinine 90 µmol/L or more, proteinuria), liver (transaminases above 40 IU/L, capsule stretch → epigastric/RUQ pain), brain (headache, visual disturbance, clonus, eclampsia, stroke), blood (platelets below 150 × 10⁹/L, haemolysis), placenta (fetal growth restriction, abnormal Doppler, stillbirth).
Severe hypertension (160/110 or higher) risks intracerebral haemorrhage and is treated urgently.
Delivery of the placenta is the only cure; disease can present or worsen after birth.

symptoms: Often asymptomatic (detected at routine BP check).
Severe headache, visual disturbance (blurring, flashing lights, scotomata).
Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting.
Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet; breathlessness (pulmonary oedema).
physicalSigns: BP 140/90 mmHg or higher; severe 160/110 mmHg or higher.
Proteinuria on dipstick (confirm with PCR or ACR).
Epigastric/liver tenderness; reduced urine output; small-for-dates uterus.
redFlags: Headache, visual scotomata, epigastric pain, vomiting, clonus — impending eclampsia
Platelets below 150 × 10⁹/L, rising creatinine (90 µmol/L or more) or ALT (above 70 IU/L or 2× ULN) → admit
precipitants: First pregnancy; previous pre-eclampsia; multiple pregnancy.
Chronic hypertension, CKD, diabetes, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome.
Age 40 or over; BMI 35 or more; family history.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Present before 20 weeks or already treated.
New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or organ dysfunction.
Hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia; overlaps with HELLP.

differentials.condition: TTP/HUS, lupus flare, epilepsy, cerebral venous thrombosis
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Seizures or thrombocytopenia from other causes.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: 140/90 or higher = hypertension; 160/110 or higher = severe.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Treat to target 135/85 mmHg; never let severe hypertension go untreated.

clinicalManagement.title: Prevention
actions: Aspirin 75–150 mg once daily from 12 weeks until birth if 1 high-risk factor (previous hypertensive pregnancy, CKD, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension) or more than 1 moderate risk factor (first pregnancy, age 40 or over, interval above 10 years, BMI 35 or more, family history, multiple pregnancy).
Stop ACE inhibitors/ARBs (within 2 working days of pregnancy confirmation) and switch.

clinicalManagement.title: Hypertension — non-severe (140/90 to 159/109)
actions: Treat chronic, gestational and pre-eclampsia hypertension above 140/90; target 135/85 mmHg.
First-line labetalol; nifedipine if labetalol unsuitable (e.g. asthma); methyldopa if neither suitable (NICE).

MOH oral doses: labetalol 100–400 mg two to three times daily (max 1200 mg/day); nifedipine 10–20 mg two to three times daily (max 180 mg/day); methyldopa 250–500 mg two to four times daily (max 2 g/day).
Pre-eclampsia: admit if any concern (severe BP, abnormal bloods, impending eclampsia, fetal compromise); consider fullPIERS/PREP-S.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe hypertension (160/110 or higher)
actions: Admit; treat until below 160/110 then to 135/85.
Labetalol 20 mg IV, then 20–80 mg every 30 min, or infusion 1–2 mg/min, maximum 300 mg, then switch to oral (MOH).
Or oral nifedipine 10 mg every 45 min, maximum 80 mg/day (MOH).
Or hydralazine 5 mg IV, repeat 5–10 mg every 30 min, maximum 20 mg (MOH); give up to 500 mL crystalloid before/with the first dose (NICE).
Limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL/h in severe pre-eclampsia (NICE).

clinicalManagement.title: Magnesium sulfate
actions: Give if eclampsia, or severe pre-eclampsia with birth planned within 24 h, or severe features (headache, scotomata, vomiting, epigastric pain, oliguria with severe hypertension, worsening bloods).
Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen: 4 g IV over 5–15 min, then 1 g/h for 24 h (24 h after the last fit). Recurrent fit: further 2–4 g over 5–15 min (NICE). MOH: 4–6 g over 15–20 min then 1–2 g/h.
Monitor reflexes, RR, SpO2, urine output; toxicity → stop and give calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10%) IV over 5–10 min.
Do not use diazepam or phenytoin instead of magnesium for eclampsia.
Call for help, left lateral, airway, oxygen; magnesium loading dose; control BP; stabilise then plan birth.

clinicalManagement.title: Timing of birth (pre-eclampsia)
actions: Before 34 weeks: continue surveillance unless indications for birth; give IV magnesium sulfate and antenatal corticosteroids if early birth planned.
34 to 36+6 weeks: surveillance unless indications; weigh maternal/fetal condition and neonatal cot availability.
37 weeks onwards: initiate birth within 24–48 h.
Do not use steroids to treat HELLP.

clinicalManagement.title: Postnatal care
actions: Measure BP daily for 2 days, once on days 3–5, and when treatment changes; target below 140/90.
Stop methyldopa within 2 days of birth; enalapril first-line postnatally (check creatinine and potassium); nifedipine or amlodipine for women of Black African/Caribbean origin.
Review at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks.

contraindications: Syndrome of asthma, rhinitis and nasal polyps

learningObjectives: Diagnose and classify hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and treat severe hypertension and eclampsia safely.
pitfalls: Diazepam or phenytoin instead of magnesium.
keyPoints: Aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks for high-risk women.
Treat 140/90 and above; target 135/85; severe 160/110 is an emergency.
Labetalol first, nifedipine if asthma, methyldopa third.
Magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/h for 24 h.
Birth at 37 weeks for pre-eclampsia; enalapril postnatally.
